extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, screenplay students, and writers of film/visual narratives
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing cinematic characters, dialogue, description, and image systems for screenplays — how to render story elements visually and auditorily for film. Emphasizes cinematic convention (visual first), economy, present-tense vividness, and recurring image motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love your characters / avoid melodrama and stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can’t love them, don’t write them. Permit neither your empathy nor antipathy for a character to produce melodrama or stereotype. Love them all without losing your clearheadedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers who 'love' their characters notice truthful, surprising details; avoid sentimentalizing or reducing characters to clichés. Empathy should inform complexity, not produce caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character is self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The root of all fine character writing is self-knowledge: 'When you ask yourself, If I were this character in these circumstances, what would I do? the honest answer is always correct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penetrate your own humanity to understand others. Use personal insight to inform believable motivations and universal human reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build characters from observed parts, don't copy life directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe life and collect bits of manner, wit, cruelty, persistence, etc., then assemble characters 'like Dr. Frankenstein' from parts rather than attempting to recreate entire real people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create dimensions of contradiction by combining distinct observed traits; this yields clearer, more archetypal characters than direct transcription of real people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Villains must be believable and self-justifying
rubrics_metrics.description: If your character’s up to no good and you place yourself within his being, you'd do everything possible to get away with it—so you would not act like a cartoon villain. 'No one thinks they’re bad.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid twirling-mustache villainy. Make antagonists charming, internally rational, or seemingly sympathetic; ground villainy in plausible self-justification (Lee Marvin example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue is not conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Real conversation is full of pauses, non sequiturs, repetitions; screen dialogue must have the swing of everyday talk but content well above normal—it is not mere eavesdropping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue should suggest subtext and relationship functions rather than mimic banal chit-chat. The scene's text is not the subtext—write for what lies beneath actual words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue: compression and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Screen dialogue must say the maximum in the fewest possible words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim flab; break exposition into short, simply constructed lines that the audience can grasp instantly. Example: replace a long expository sentence with a string of short informal lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue: direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Each exchange of dialogue must turn the beats of the scene in one direction or another across changing behaviors, without repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each line moves the scene forward or shifts relationships/emotion; avoid repetitive exchanges that stall dramatic momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue: purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Each line or exchange of dialogue executes a step in design that builds and arcs the scene around its Turning Point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write dialogue that performs design work — reveals character, raises stakes, pivots the scene toward its turning point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak as common people do, think as wise men do
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue must sound informal and natural (contractions, slang, profanity if needed) while carrying intelligent subtext.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use everyday vocabulary but ensure the thought behind the line is wise and purposeful; avoid overwriting with literary flourishes that feel unnatural for speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, simply constructed sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Screen dialogue demands short, simply constructed sentences—generally a movement from noun to verb to object or complement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long, nested expository sentences; prefer short punches and colloquial phrasing that actors and audiences instantly process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue can omit grammatical completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue doesn’t require complete sentences—open articles or pronouns are often dropped; speech can be phrase-based or grunts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write as people actually talk on-screen: fragments, ellipses, and interrupted lines are acceptable and often desirable for realism and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read dialogue aloud and avoid clever or self-conscious lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your dialogue out loud or into a tape recorder to avoid tongue twisters, accidental rhymes, alliterations, or anything that calls attention to itself as 'clever.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a line shouts 'Oh, what a clever line am I!' cut it. Favor naturalness over literary showmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short speeches (stikomythia) over long monologues
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of screen dialogue is rapid exchange of short speeches; long speeches are antithetical to the aesthetics of cinema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid columns of dialogue; break speeches to respect visual attention span (ten–fifteen seconds). Use action/reaction patterns to fragment monologues; include silent reactions and parentheticals to shape beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show action/reaction dynamics, not prepared monologues
rubrics_metrics.description: Life is always action/reaction—no monologues or prepared speeches. The speaker’s next lines depend on the listener’s reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes as improvisations: fragment speech with reactions (listener’s silence, looks, gestures) that change the speaker's beat. Use parentheticals and beats to indicate these shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the suspense (periodic) sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellent film dialogue tends to shape itself into the periodic or 'suspense sentence' whose meaning is delayed until the final word, forcing attention to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure many lines so the key noun/gesture/idea arrives at the end, increasing actor/audience focus (example: 'If you didn’t want me to do it, why'd you give me that . . .').

rubrics_metrics.name: The Silent Screenplay: prefer visual over verbal
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write a line of dialogue when you can create a visual expression. Image first; dialogue is the regretful second choice. Obey the Law of Diminishing Returns: the more dialogue you write, the less effect dialogue has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attack scenes looking for purely visual ways to tell them. Make dialogue lean so it stands out against visual storytelling (Bergman waiter example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe only what can be photographed
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly ask: 'What do I see on the screen?' and describe only what is photographic; ninety percent of verbal expression has no filmic equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace non-photographable lines ('He’s been sitting there for a long time') with concrete visual actions ('He stubs out his tenth cigarette', 'He nervously glances at his watch').

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in present tense with vivid action in the now
rubrics_metrics.description: The ontology of the screen is absolute present tense in constant vivid movement—screenplay is written in present tense because film is on the knife edge of the now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey relentless action; even static shots must feel alive. Use active present-tense verbs to create immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific, concrete nouns and active verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: To write vividly, avoid generic nouns and verbs with adjectives/adverbs; seek the most specific name of the thing (e.g., 'The carpenter hammers a spike' not 'uses a big nail').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace bland verbs/adjectives ('starts to move slowly') with vivid verbs ('pads', 'ambles', 'staggers', etc.) to create distinct imagery and precise character action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate forms of 'to be' (is/are/it is) where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate 'is' and 'are' throughout; onscreen nothing is in a state of being—story life is flux and becoming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite passive or static descriptions into active present-tense behavior to make scenes cinematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphor/simile that cannot be photographed
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate all metaphor and simile that cannot pass the test 'What do I see (or hear) onscreen?'—in film, 'a tree is a tree.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphor/simile only when it can be realized visually or aurally on screen; avoid director traps and unphotographable poetic excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate 'we see' / 'we hear' constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'We' doesn’t exist in a screenplay—'we see' injects an image of the crew and shatters the reader's vision of the film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write directly: 'A truck splashes through a puddle', not 'We see a truck splash through a puddle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove camera and editing notations from the script
rubrics_metrics.description: Delete 'CUT TO', 'PAN TO', 'RACK FOCUS', etc.; the reader assumes changes of angle are done on a cut. Directors laugh at attempts to direct from the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit specific camera/editing instructions to only those absolutely necessary for storytelling; rely on description and writing to suggest angle/distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master Scene technique: include only essential angles and suggest composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The contemporary screenplay is a Master Scene work including only angles essential to telling the story. Suggest angles by breaking paragraphs into descriptive units that imply camera distance and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mini-paragraphs/white space to lead the reader’s inner eye through wide shots, close-ups, inserts, and character gestures without explicit camera labels. Use INSERT/ON SCENE sparingly when audience must see specific objects (note example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image Systems: build recurring, subtle motif strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: An IMAGE SYSTEM is a strategy of motifs—categories of imagery that repeat in sight and sound from beginning to end with persistence and variation to subliminally enrich meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a category (nature, machines, seasons, animals, objects) and repeat appropriate images with variation and subtlety. Avoid isolated symbols; the power comes from organized return and invisibility to conscious notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: External vs Internal Imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: External Imagery imports already-known symbolic meanings (flag = patriotism); Internal Imagery assigns new, film-specific meaning to a category (water becomes death in LES DIABOLIQUE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to rely on conventional symbols or to construct an internal symbolic language unique to the film; be deliberate and consistent in usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude most reality; select objects for connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step to poetic film is to exclude 90 percent of reality; only objects with appropriate connotations for the film should remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully choose props and mise-en-scène (what kind of vase, where placed, lit, touched) because each object is highly charged and relates to every other object and the film’s meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetics must be handled with virtual invisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A film’s poetics (image systems, motifs) should communicate subliminally and go consciously unrecognized while enriching depth and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overt, decorative 'pretty pictures' that distract from core human content; ensure poetic imagery serves thematic and emotional expressivity rather than mere beauty.
